TextBlock.Text: Sunday, 16 April 2028 | European Edition | No. 21,884 | 2.80 EUR
Alliance cannot agree what to call it

StackPanel.TextBlock:
COPENHAGEN / BRUSSELS — The standing maritime group that has patrolled the North Sea for the past four years has stopped answering its own headquarters.
In a signal transmitted in clear at 0400 on Saturday and picked up by every merchant in the Kattegat, the group’s commander, Konteradmiral Reimar Vahl, announced that the Baltic approaches were closed to naval traffic and would remain closed “until the alliance is prepared to decide something.”
The declaration follows five weeks of consultations that produced no agreed response to the sabotage of three undersea cables and a gas interconnector in the eastern Baltic. A communique described the attacks as “a matter of grave concern.” No further measures were announced.
Vahl’s squadron consists of ships contributed by several member states and remains, on paper, an allied formation. Officials in three capitals spent Saturday disagreeing over whether the correct word is mutiny, and one senior officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the more difficult question was whether the admiral was wrong.
“He has not fired on anyone,” the officer said. “He has done in one morning what we failed to do in five weeks, which is force a decision. That is exactly the problem.”
A second allied formation, reported as Task Group NORTHWIND, was ordered to sea from Wilhelmshaven late on Saturday. Its orders have not been made public.

War-risk cover for hulls transiting the Skagerrak and the Belts was withdrawn within nine hours of the signal. Rates for the few underwriters still quoting have risen roughly elevenfold.
Two hundred and forty ships were in the approaches at the time of the announcement. Most are still there. Masters have been advised to hold position and keep their transponders on.

Naval analysts note that both formations operate the same classes of ship, the same sensors and the same recognition procedures.
“There is no technical way to tell them apart at sea,” one former staff officer said. “Whoever is sent up there will be looking at his own fleet through his own radar and guessing.”
